# Balancing Moisture in a Small Compost Bin

A balcony compost bin that smells sour is often described as “too wet,” but the useful diagnosis also considers air pockets, particle size, and the ratio of fresh scraps to dry structure. Adding a handful of paper can help; burying the problem under an entire newspaper may create a dry lid over a wet center.

## Inspect layers

Wear gloves and turn a small section. Material should feel like a wrung sponge, with no liquid pooling at the bottom. Matted grass and large wet food pieces exclude air. Break them apart and mix in torn cardboard, dry leaves, or coarse stems throughout the active layer.

## Change inputs for a week

Pause watery scraps, drain coffee grounds, and cut new material smaller. Note temperature, odor, visible insects, and how quickly the top layer changes. If the bin remains cold and unchanged, moisture may not be the only limit; volume and seasonal temperature matter too.

## Harvest without resetting everything

Move unfinished material to one side and remove only dark, crumbly compost that smells earthy. Keep a small active portion to seed the next batch. Balcony herbs can use mature compost sparingly, as described in [[07-balcony-herbs|Herbs Share a Balcony, Not a Watering Schedule]].

The aim is a recoverable process, not an odor-free display at every moment. A short log of inputs and corrections makes the next imbalance easier to interpret.
